standard.goal: An architecture document says how the product delivers its UX, as a framework and principles. The framework is the product's parts and how they relate. Each principle comes with its reason, so a builder applies it to a case it did not foresee. The framework and the principles hold as long as the UX stays, whatever the implementation. Whoever builds or changes the product, a person or an AI, derives each part's specification from the document and implements it. Because every builder works from the same framework and principles, they do not hesitate over each part, and every part is made on the same thinking. So the product stays readable, maintainable and resilient to change.

template.skeleton:
# <Product name> architecture

<How the product delivers its UX, in a sentence or two, with a link to the UX>

## Principles

<A link to the principles of the architecture this one is built on, where there is one>

### <A short name for the principle>

<The rule every part is built by, in a sentence>

<Its reason: what the rule is there for, and what goes wrong for the user or the builder without it>

## User stories

- As <the user>, I want <one way they use the product at its edge, such as a command they run>. Carries <the UX's scenarios, or their steps, that rest on it>.

## Logical view

### Components

<One SVG figure in the notation of a C4 component diagram: a box for each role the user stories need and each store of data, holding its name and a tag of its type and technology, such as "[web app · React, TypeScript]" or "[database · PostgreSQL]", and no sentence; the box's shape saying its kind of element, such as a person, an app or a store of data; an arrow from each to the one it acts on, labelled with what it does and the data it hands on, named as in the data model, and with the protocol where it matters, such as "[HTTPS/JSON]"; a legend of the shapes and the tags; the boxes placed so the arrows run in the order they act and cross none>

- <What a role alone is responsible for that no arrow shows>
- <A choice the figure shows that the reader would question, such as a technology, with why it was made over the other way>

### Data model

<One SVG figure in the notation of an ER diagram: a box for each data the roles pass or keep, holding its name alone; a line between two data for each relation between them, labelled with the relation's name, its ends drawn in crow's-foot notation for its cardinality, such as one to many>

### Sequences

<For each user story, a UML sequence diagram in Mermaid: a participant for the user, for each role the story reaches, named as in Components, and for each thing outside the product it reaches; a message for each step, labelled in a few words with what one does and the data handed on, named as in the data model>

- <A choice the diagrams show that the reader would question, with why it was made over the other way>

## Physical view

### Deployment

<One SVG figure in the notation of a C4 deployment diagram: an outer box for each execution environment, such as a cloud service, a phone, the user's computer or CI, with its technology tag; inside it a box for each deployment unit, such as an app or a container, named with its technology tag, holding by their names, as in Components, the roles that run in it and the data kept in it; a box for each thing outside the product they depend on, with an arrow labelled with what is used>

- <How the product is started>
- <A choice the figure shows that the reader would question, such as a technology, with why it was made over the other way>

### Directory structure

```text
<A tree of the folders and files of the product; each line that holds a role or a data names it as in Components, with its technology tag>
```

## Test

<A link to the project's shared test rules, where it has them; what follows says only what differs from them>

| Deployment unit | Unit | Integration | End-to-end |
|---|---|---|---|
| <Each deployment unit, named as in Deployment with its technology tag> | <Tool · weight, such as ●●● or ●●○ · what it checks, in a few words> | <The same> | <The same, or ▨ and a footnote mark where the cell is empty> |

[^1]: <Why the cell is empty>

- <Each deployment unit left out because every cell of its row would be empty, with why>
- Unit tests: <what they make real and what they fake>. Pass: <the criteria>
- Integration tests: <what they make real and what they fake>. Pass: <the criteria>
- End-to-end tests: <what they make real and what they fake>. Pass: <the criteria>
- <Each other test type the product needs, such as a performance test>: <what it makes real and what it fakes>. Pass: <the criteria; for a result that varies from run to run, how many runs of how many must meet the expectation>
- <Each deployment unit's weight, with what a failure of it would cost the user>
- <A choice the table shows that the reader would question, such as a tool, with why it was made over the other way>

parts.what: The title, and the sentence or two under it, with a link to the UX.
parts.why: The builder holds the one idea of how the product delivers its UX before reading the rest, and builds each part as a piece of it.

parts.what: One subsection for each principle, holding the rule and its reason, after a link to the principles of the architecture this one is built on, where there is one.
parts.why: The builder decides each detail by the rules every part is built by, and decides a case no rule names from a rule's reason.

parts.what: A list under its heading, one item for each story, each naming the UX's scenarios or steps that rest on it.
parts.why: The builder sees each way the user uses the product at its edge, and draws the roles and the data from them.

parts.what: The figure under Components, an SVG file beside the document drawn by hand in the notation of a C4 component diagram: each box a role's or a store's name and a tag of its type and technology, its shape saying its kind of element, each arrow what one does to another with the data and the protocol where it matters, and a legend.
parts.why: The builder sees, at a glance, the roles to build, what each is made with, and what each does to which.

parts.what: The first items of the list under Components: what a role alone is responsible for that no arrow shows.
parts.why: The builder finds the rest of a role's responsibility next to the figure, without the box being read as text.

parts.what: The items of the lists under Components, Sequences, Deployment and Test that give a choice the reader would question, such as a technology or a tool, with why.
parts.why: The builder finds why a choice they question was made, next to the figure that shows it.

parts.what: The figure under Data model, an SVG file beside the document drawn by hand in the notation of an ER diagram: each box a data's name, each line a relation's name with its cardinality.
parts.why: The builders of the role that writes a data and of the role that reads it take each relation, and how many of each it joins, the same way.

parts.what: The UML sequence diagrams in Mermaid under Sequences, one for each user story; a sequence has one layout, its order down the page, so Mermaid draws it from text.
parts.why: The builder follows each story through the roles, in order, with the data each hands on.

parts.what: The figure under Deployment, an SVG file beside the document drawn by hand in the notation of a C4 deployment diagram: each outer box an execution environment, holding the deployment units, each with its technology tag and the roles and data in it; and the list under it, of how the product is started and of choices.
parts.why: The builder puts each role and each data in the deployment unit and the environment where it runs or is kept, and starts the product.

parts.what: The tree under Directory structure, in text, as the files lie, each line that holds a role or a data naming it as in Components with its technology tag.
parts.why: The builder finds the one place to make or change each role and each data.

parts.what: The table under Test: a row for each deployment unit, a column for each test type from narrow scope to wide, unit, integration and end-to-end; each cell a tool, a weight and what it checks in a few words, an empty cell hatched with a footnote; and the note of the units left out.
parts.why: The builder sees at a glance which unit is tested by which type of test, how heavily and with what, and why a cell is empty.

parts.what: The lines under the table: for each test type, including any the product adds, what it makes real, what it fakes and when it passes; each unit's weight with what a failure costs the user; and a link to the project's shared test rules, with only what differs written here.
parts.why: The builder writes each test with the right neighbours real or faked, knows when the tests pass, and knows why a unit is tested as heavily as it is.

checklist.what: When a colleague asks "How does the product deliver its UX?", can the builder answer in a sentence or two?
checklist.why: If yes, the builder holds the one idea every part comes from, and builds each part as a piece of it, so the parts fit together as one design. The link to the UX tells the builder which experience the parts must deliver. If no, the builder meets the parts one by one, cannot tell which part carries the idea, and builds each on its own thinking.
grounds: Brooks, The Mythical Man-Month (1975): "I will contend that conceptual integrity is the most important consideration in system design."
arc42, section 4 "Solution Strategy": "A short summary and explanation of the fundamental decisions and solution strategies, that shape the system's architecture."

examples.fails: RoomBook is built on a modern, scalable cloud architecture.
examples.passes: RoomBook reads the meeting a worker describes, matches it to the rooms whose seats and equipment fit, and asks the office calendar which of them are free, so the worker is offered only rooms that fit. The UX it delivers is in ux.md.

checklist.what: When two builders, each making a different role, meet the same case the document does not name, does one principle's reason settle it the same way for both?
checklist.why: If yes, each builder decides a case the document did not foresee as its writer would have, because the principle says what it is there for, and every role is made on the same thinking, so the user meets one product. A principle is a rule every part is built by; a means, such as a language or a tool, is not one. If no, a rule with no reason is stretched to a case it was not meant for or ignored where it was, a decision every role meets with no principle to cover it is made one way in one role and another way in the next, and a principle each reads their own way, such as "keep it simple", settles nothing. The user then meets two behaviours where they expect one.
grounds: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010:2011, 3.2: architecture is the "fundamental concepts or properties of a system in its environment embodied in its elements, relationships, and in the principles of its design and evolution".
arc42, section 8 "Crosscutting Concepts": "Such concepts are often related to multiple building blocks."

Anthropic, "Prompting best practices" (Claude Platform Docs), Add context to improve performance: "Providing context or motivation behind your instructions, such as explaining to Claude why such behavior is important, can give Claude more information about your goals and help it deliver more targeted responses." and "Claude can generalize from the explanation."

examples.fails: No principle says what to do when Google Workspace does not answer. (The builder of the Room matcher offers every room that fits; the builder of the Booking page shows an error. The worker gets a list one day and an error the next.)
examples.passes: Principle: RoomBook never offers a room it has not seen free. Reason: a room offered and then found taken spoils the meeting it was booked for. (Both builders show that rooms cannot be checked now, and offer none.)

checklist.what: For each step of each of the UX's scenarios, can the builder name the user story that carries it?
checklist.why: If yes, every step the user takes reaches the product by one way of using it at its edge, and the roles drawn from the stories deliver the whole UX. If no, a step no story carries is built by guess or not at all, and the user meets a gap where the UX promised a step.
grounds: arc42, section 3 "Context and Scope": "Context and scope - as the name suggests - delimits your system (i.e. your scope) from all its communication partners".

Kruchten, "Architectural Blueprints—The “4+1” View Model of Software Architecture", IEEE Software, 1995, on the scenarios: "as a driver to discover the architectural elements during the architecture design".

examples.fails: As an office worker, I want to book a room. Carries O1. (No story carries the UX's step where the worker describes the meeting and gets the rooms that fit, so the builder makes a plain list of every room.)
examples.passes: As an office worker, I want to describe my meeting and get the rooms that fit it. Carries O1, steps 1-2. As an office worker, I want to book one of them and find it in my calendar. Carries O1, steps 3-4.

checklist.what: When the builder starts on a role, can they begin making it without choosing for themselves what it is made with?
checklist.why: If yes, every role of one kind is made the same way, and the builder starts at once: the tag in the role's box names its type, such as a service or a module, and its technology. If no, each builder picks their own language or framework, so one kind of role is made two ways and the next builder must know both, or a role relies on what the place it runs does not have.
grounds: C4 model, "Notation": "The type of every element should be explicitly specified (e.g. Person, Software System, Container or Component)." and "Every container and component should have a technology explicitly specified."

examples.fails: Every box holds a name alone. (The builder of the Room matcher writes it in TypeScript beside the Booking page; the Booking API, in Python, cannot call it in-process.)
examples.passes: "Booking page [web app · React, TypeScript]", "Booking API [service · Python, FastAPI]", "Meeting reader [module · Python, Claude API]", "Room matcher [module · Python]" and "Calendar link [module · Python]".

checklist.what: When the builder asks of anything the user stories need decided, "Which role decides this?", can they point to exactly one role?
checklist.why: If yes, each thing is decided once, in one role, and a change to it is made in that role alone. A role's responsibility shows in what it does to the others, and the list under the figure holds what no arrow carries. Roles split by a responsibility of their own, not by function, by stage of processing or to fit a technology. If no, a thing decided in two roles is decided two ways by their two builders, and one decided in none is decided by guess wherever it is first needed.
grounds: Parnas, "On the Criteria To Be Used in Decomposing Systems into Modules" (1972): "one begins with a list of difficult design decisions or design decisions which are likely to change. Each module is then designed to hide such a decision from the others."

examples.fails: Three boxes, Frontend, Backend and Database, joined by arrows labelled "API" and "SQL". (Asked which role decides whether a room fits, the builder can point to Frontend or to Backend.)
examples.passes: The Booking API "asks for rooms that fit" the Room matcher, with the Meeting request, and the list under the figure says the Room matcher alone decides a fit: a seat for each attendee and the equipment the meeting asks for.

checklist.what: When one builder makes the role that writes a data and another makes the role that reads it, do they take the way the data join the same way?
checklist.why: If yes, the two roles work together the first time they meet, as each relation is drawn once, named, with how many of one go with one of the other (its cardinality) at its ends, and both read it. If no, a relation no figure draws, or one drawn without how many it joins, is made one way by the role that writes it and read another way by the role that reads it, and the fault shows only when the two run together.
grounds: Mermaid, "Entity Relationship Diagrams": "Cardinality is a property that describes how many elements of another entity can be related to the entity in question."

examples.fails: Boxes Meeting request, Room and Booking, with a plain line from Booking to Room. (The Booking page stores several rooms in one booking, while the Calendar link books only the first.)
examples.passes: A line from Booking to Room named "holds", with crow's-foot ends for many bookings to one room; a line from Booking to Meeting request named "is for", one to one.

checklist.what: When the builder traces one user story, can they follow it from the user's first request to its end, each step done by a role, with the data that role hands on?
checklist.why: If yes, the builder sees that the roles together carry each story, not only each its own share, and builds each role knowing which steps it does, what it receives and what it hands on. Each message names its role as Components does and its data as the data model does, and runs along an arrow of Components, which gives its protocol, so both ends of it are built to meet. If no, a step no role does is found only when the story is built, and is added to whichever role is nearest, by guess; a data the builder cannot follow from the role that makes it to the role that uses it is made in one form and read in another.
grounds: arc42, section 6 "Runtime View": "The runtime view describes concrete behavior and interactions of the system's building blocks in form of scenarios".
Mermaid, "Sequence diagrams": "A Sequence diagram is an interaction diagram that shows how processes operate with one another and in what order."

examples.fails: Browser ->> Server: request; Server -->> Browser: response. (The step where the worker finds the booking in their calendar is done by no role, so the builder of the Booking page adds a calendar call of its own.)
examples.passes: Worker ->> Booking page: books a room; Booking page ->> Booking API: booking; Booking API ->> Calendar link: booking; Calendar link ->> Google Workspace: puts the booking on the room's and the worker's calendars; Booking API -->> Booking page: booking confirmed.

checklist.what: When the builder sets the product up from nothing, can they get it running, each role and each data in its place, without asking anyone?
checklist.why: If yes, the builder knows where each role runs, and so what it can reach and when a change to it reaches the user, and where each data is kept, and so who can read it and whether it outlives a run. Each deployment unit sits in the environment it runs in, holding its roles and data, each with its technology, and each thing outside the product the roles depend on is drawn, as it is where the product breaks for the user first. The list under the figure says how the product is started. If no, the builder places a role or a data by guess, and finds what it cannot reach only once it runs.
grounds: arc42, section 7 "Deployment view": "Software does not run without hardware."
C4 model, "Deployment diagram": "A deployment node represents where an instance of a software system/container is running."

examples.fails: RoomBook runs in the cloud. (The builder of the Calendar link cannot tell where it runs, whether that place can reach Google Workspace, nor where bookings are kept.)
examples.passes: Outer box "Google Cloud [Cloud Run, Cloud SQL]" holds "Booking page app [Cloud Run service · React, TypeScript]", "Booking API container [Cloud Run service · Python, FastAPI]", which holds Booking API, Meeting reader, Room matcher and Calendar link, and "Room store [Cloud SQL · PostgreSQL]". Outside: Google Workspace "room free times, bookings [HTTPS]" and the Claude API "reads meetings [HTTPS]". Under it: a worker starts RoomBook by opening its page.

checklist.what: When the builder makes or changes a role or a data, can they put its files in the one place they belong, without asking anyone?
checklist.why: If yes, the builder makes each role and each data where it is kept, and the place tells who owns it. If no, a role kept in no place is put where the builder guesses, and one kept in two places is made twice and drifts.
grounds: GitHub Docs, "About code owners": "You can use a CODEOWNERS file to define individuals or teams that are responsible for code in a repository."
Hunt and Thomas, The Pragmatic Programmer (1999), DRY: "Every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system."

examples.passes: web/ Booking page [React, TypeScript]; api/main.py Booking API [Python, FastAPI]; api/reader/ Meeting reader [Python, Claude API]; api/matcher/ Room matcher [Python]; api/calendar/ Calendar link [Python]; db/schema.sql Room store [PostgreSQL].

checklist.what: When a colleague asks "Is anything in this product left untested?", can the builder answer, for each deployment unit, which types of test from unit to end-to-end cover it, and why a type is missing where it is?
checklist.why: If yes, the builder sees that every deployment unit is tested from narrow scope to wide, or why not: unit tests take its roles one at a time, integration tests join it to its real neighbours, and end-to-end tests run the whole as the user does. An empty cell has its reason in a footnote. If no, a unit with no row, or an empty cell with no reason, goes untested unseen, and many narrow tests with no wide one pass while a user story fails.
grounds: Vocke, "The Practical Test Pyramid" (martinfowler.com), on Cohn's pyramid: "Write tests with different granularity" and "The more high-level you get the fewer tests you should have".
Winters, Manshreck and Wright, Software Engineering at Google, ch. 11 "Testing Overview": "Scope refers to the specific code paths we are verifying."

examples.fails: Every module is unit tested to 80% coverage. (No row for the whole on staging, and nothing says why the Booking page has no integration test.)
examples.passes:
| Booking page app [Cloud Run service · React, TypeScript] | Vitest ●○○ form, room list | Playwright, API faked ●○○ pages against the API | ▨[^1] |
| Booking API container [Cloud Run service · Python, FastAPI] | pytest ●●● fit rules, handlers | pytest, real PostgreSQL, Workspace faked ●●○ queries, calendar calls | ▨[^1] |
| RoomBook on staging [Cloud Run] | ▨[^2] | ▨[^2] | Playwright on GitHub Actions ●●○ booking story, test calendar |
[^1]: end-to-end runs on the whole alone. [^2]: the units it is made of are tested in their own rows.

checklist.what: When the builder writes a test of one type, such as an integration test, can they write it without deciding for themselves what to make real and what to fake?
checklist.why: If yes, every test of a type stands on the same ground, set once in the line for its type under the table, so a failing test points to the part it is about. If no, one builder's integration test fakes the database and another's does not, so a fault passes one and fails the other, and the two disagree on what broke.
grounds: Vocke, "The Practical Test Pyramid" (martinfowler.com): "For your automated tests this means you don't just need to run your own application but also the component you're integrating with." and "it's totally okay to come up with other names for your test layers, as long as you keep it consistent within your codebase and your team's discussions."

examples.fails: Integration tests: test the API with its dependencies. (Is Google Workspace real? Is PostgreSQL?)
examples.passes: Integration tests: the container and PostgreSQL are real; Google Workspace and the Claude API are faked.

checklist.what: When the builder has run the tests of a deployment unit, can they say whether it passes without setting the bar themselves?
checklist.why: If yes, every builder stops at the same bar, set once for each type of test, so a unit passes for every builder or for none. A test whose result varies from run to run has its bar as how many runs of how many must meet the expectation. If no, each builder sets their own bar, so a unit passes for one and fails for another, and a test that met its expectation once is taken as working.
grounds: Schwaber and Sutherland, The Scrum Guide (2020): "The Definition of Done is a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product."

examples.fails: Unit tests: good coverage. Integration tests: they should pass.
examples.passes: Unit tests: all pass; line and branch coverage at least 90%; at ●●●, property tests pass and the mutation score is at least 95%. Integration tests: all pass on a fresh database.

checklist.what: When the builder doubts a choice the document makes, such as a technology or how heavily a unit is tested, can they tell what would be lost by taking the other way?
checklist.why: If yes, the builder keeps the choice or changes it knowing what it was for, since its reason stands beside the figure or the table that shows it. A unit's weight is weighed by what a failure of it would cost the user of this product. If no, a later builder can only keep the choice blindly, or change it blindly and undo what it was for; a reason such as "it is the core" names nothing that would be lost.
grounds: Nygard, "Documenting Architecture Decisions" (2011): without the motivation, a new team member can only "Blindly accept the decision." or "Blindly change it."
Ubl, "Design Docs at Google": "The design doc is the place to write down the trade-offs you made in designing your software."

examples.fails: Deployment tags the Room store "[Cloud SQL · PostgreSQL]", and nothing says why it is not a database the team runs. The Booking API container is ●●●: it is the core.
examples.passes: Under Deployment: Cloud SQL rather than a database run by the team, so backups and failover need no one on call; RoomBook's team has none. Under Test: Booking API container ●●●, as a wrong match puts a six-person review in a four-seat room.

checklist.what: When the builder asks of any user story, role or data "Which step of the UX needs this?", can they answer?
checklist.why: If yes, the framework grows and shrinks with the UX alone: the builder keeps what a step needs, and removes a role once the steps that needed it are gone. If no, a role no step needs is built, kept and tested by every builder after, and stays on because no one can tell whether removing it breaks anything; a story for a step inside the product adds roles without the user doing more.
grounds: IEEE Std 830-1998, 4.3.8 "Traceable": "Backward traceability (i.e., to previous stages of development). This depends upon each requirement explicitly referencing its source in earlier documents."

Fowler, "Yagni" (martinfowler.com, 2015): "The code for the presumptive feature adds some complexity to the software, this complexity makes it harder to modify and debug that software, thus increasing the cost of other features."

examples.fails: A role, Notification hub, that no user story's sequence reaches. (A builder cannot tell whether removing it breaks anything, so it is kept and tested on every change.)
examples.passes: Every role in Components is reached in the sequence of a story, and each story names the steps of the UX it carries.

checklist.what: When the builder changes how a role works inside, such as its steps, its behaviour in one case or a data's fields, while the UX and the principles stay, does every line of the document still hold?
checklist.why: If yes, the builder chooses the best way to build each role and changes it freely, and the document stays true for every builder after them. How a role behaves in each case is decided where it is built, such as in its tests, and a data's fields are decided where the data is built. If no, a line that holds such a detail, such as a count, a value or a role's steps, is decided again where the role is built, drifts from it, and is followed by the next builder as if it still held.
grounds: Ubl, "Design Docs at Google": "A clear indicator that a doc might not be necessary are design docs that are really implementation manuals."

Parnas, "On the Criteria To Be Used in Decomposing Systems into Modules" (1972): "one begins with a list of difficult design decisions or design decisions which are likely to change. Each module is then designed to hide such a decision from the others."

examples.fails: Under Components: "The Room matcher reads rooms with one SQL join, caches the result for five minutes, and retries Google Workspace three times." (Moving the cache or the retry into the Calendar link leaves these lines untrue.)
examples.passes: Under Components: "The Room matcher offers a room only when it is free for the whole meeting." The Room matcher's queries, caching and retries change, and the line still holds.
